title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
description: Brute force to optimized: assigning elements to buckets independently versus sort-descending, fill-one-bucket-at-a-time backtracking with strong pruning.

content.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if it is possible to divide this array into k non-empty subsets whose sums are all equal, using every element exactly once across all subsets.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums (array of positive integers), k (number of equal-sum subsets required)"],["Output","true if such a partition exists, false otherwise"],["Goal","Determine feasibility of splitting into k groups of equal sum, using backtracking with strong pruning"],["Constraints","1 <= k <= nums.length <= 16"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Partition into k groups with equal sum\"","First compute the required target sum per group (total / k); then backtrack, filling one group at a time"],["Small n (up to 16), NP-hard-flavored partitioning","Backtracking with aggressive pruning (skip overflowing sums, skip duplicate failed attempts, sort descending first)"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Before attempting any partition, the total sum of nums must be evenly divisible by k; otherwise no equal-sum partition can exist. If it is divisible, the target sum for each of the k subsets is total/k, and the challenge becomes finding whether the elements can actually be grouped to hit that target exactly, k times.

blocks.title: Analogy: Splitting a Group of Friends' Expenses Evenly
blocks.text: Picture k friends who each paid for different items, and wanting to regroup the ITEMS (not the friends) into k bags so each bag totals the exact same amount. This problem asks whether such an equal regrouping is even possible.

blocks.caption: First check total mod k, then compute the required per-subset target sum

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Result: true. Total is 20, target per subset is 5: {4,1}, {3,2}, {2,3}, {5} all sum to 5, so 4 equal subsets exist.
5. How Should We Think?

Before trying every possible assignment of elements to k labeled buckets, notice that sorting elements DESCENDING first (so large, hard-to-place elements are handled early) and filling one bucket completely before starting the next, with aggressive pruning, dramatically reduces the search space compared to a naive bucket-by-bucket assignment.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If total sum is not evenly divisible by k, or the single largest element exceeds the target sum, the answer is immediately false, no search needed.

Observation 2: Filling ONE bucket completely (reaching exactly the target sum) before moving on to start the next bucket, rather than deciding bucket assignments for all elements simultaneously, keeps the recursive state small (just "which elements are used" and "current bucket's running sum").

Observation 3: Sorting elements in DESCENDING order before starting means large elements are placed first, when the most bucket space is available, failing fast if a large element cannot fit anywhere, a much stronger and earlier-triggered pruning signal.

Observation 4: When trying candidates for the current bucket, if adding a candidate would overflow the target sum, skip it (prune); additionally, if the CURRENT bucket is still empty and a candidate fails to lead to a solution, there is no point trying an identical-value candidate afterward (it would fail the exact same way), so that branch can be pruned immediately (implemented as a "break" when currentSum is 0, since a failing first element makes the whole partition impossible from this state, given elements are tried in a fixed order without needing to try alternate identical values).

This leads to computing the target sum per bucket, sorting nums descending, and backtracking by filling one bucket at a time, using multiple pruning rules (overflow skip, largest-element-first, empty-bucket-fail-fast) to keep the search efficient.
6. Brute Force Solution
Assign every element to one of k buckets (using k-ary choices per element), then check whether all k bucket sums come out equal to total/k.
Step by step algorithm

items: Assign every element in nums to one of k buckets (k choices per element).
After all assignments are made, compute each bucket's sum.
Return true if every bucket has an equal sum (and none are empty), for any assignment.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every element against every bucket independently explores k^n possible assignments in the worst case, without the stronger structural pruning available.
It still prunes bucket overflow, but misses the much more effective "fill one bucket completely, in descending order" strategy.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k^n) worst case, n elements each with k bucket choices.
Space: O(n) recursion depth, O(k) for the bucket sums.

Limitation: assigning elements to buckets independently, without a fixed fill-order or descending-sort strategy, misses opportunities to fail fast on large elements and prune symmetric/duplicate attempts early.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sorting descending matters: large elements are the hardest to place (fewest buckets can accommodate them without overflowing), so placing them FIRST causes infeasible branches to fail immediately, rather than after many small elements have already been placed.

Why filling one bucket completely (instead of juggling all k buckets' partial sums at once) helps: it reduces the branching decision at each step to "which remaining element goes into the CURRENT bucket," reusing the same recursive call structure once a bucket fills up and the next one starts fresh.

Why the "empty bucket, first candidate fails" pruning rule is valid: if starting a fresh bucket with the very first (largest remaining) candidate cannot lead to a solution, no other arrangement of the remaining elements into this fresh bucket can succeed either, given the fixed processing order, since every other combination for this bucket would have been reachable via a permutation of these same failed attempts.

The core idea: precompute the target, sort descending, then backtrack by filling buckets one at a time with strong pruning rules.

Sort nums descending. Backtrack: fill the current bucket by trying remaining unused elements (skipping any that would overflow the target); once a bucket reaches exactly the target sum, start a fresh bucket; succeed once k buckets are completed.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for nums = [4, 3, 2, 3, 5, 2, 1] sorted descending = [5,4,3,3,2,2,1], k=4, target=5

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bucket being filled","Elements chosen","Sum reached"],"rows":[["Bucket 1","5","5 (done)"],["Bucket 2","4, 1","5 (done)"],["Bucket 3","3, 2","5 (done)"],["Bucket 4","3, 2","5 (done) -> all 4 buckets filled, return true"]]}

blocks.caption: Sort descending, fill one bucket at a time, prune overflowing or redundant empty-bucket attempts

blocks.text: Why This Works

Filling one bucket completely before starting the next correctly explores every distinct way to partition the elements into k equal-sum groups, since the order in which buckets are filled does not affect whether a valid partition exists. Sorting descending ensures the hardest-to-place (largest) elements are considered first, so infeasible branches fail as early as possible. The empty-bucket pruning rule is valid because, given a fixed processing order, if the very first (largest available) candidate cannot lead anywhere from an empty bucket, no other choice for that position can either, since all such choices are symmetric attempts to start the bucket fresh.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(k^n) worst case in theory, but the pruning rules make this dramatically faster in practice for the given constraints (n up to 16).
Space: O(n) for the used array and recursion depth.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Assign each element to any of k buckets independently","O(k^n) worst case, weak pruning","O(n + k)","Correct, but far slower in practice without descending sort and fail-fast rules."],["Sort descending, fill one bucket at a time with strong pruning","O(k^n) worst case, fast in practice","O(n)","The expected, standard, and practically efficient solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets is a strong example of how backtracking's worst-case complexity can remain unchanged in theory, while multiple well-chosen pruning rules (descending sort, overflow skip, empty-bucket fail-fast) make it dramatically faster in practice for realistic inputs.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the early exit when total is not divisible by k, or when the largest single element exceeds the target.
Missing the empty-bucket fail-fast pruning, which is often the single most impactful optimization for this problem.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k equals nums.length","Every element must be its own subset; only possible if all elements are equal."],["k = 1","Trivially true, the entire array is the one required subset."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly stating the three key pruning rules (divisibility/largest-element check, descending sort, empty-bucket fail-fast) up front shows a strong command of backtracking optimization technique, beyond just correctness.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "partition into groups with equal sum", think: compute the target sum first, sort descending, then backtrack filling one bucket completely at a time.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you extend this to also return one valid partition, not just true/false?
How would a bitmask dynamic programming approach (over subsets of used elements) compare in complexity for larger n?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Partition Equal Subset Sum, the k=2 special case of this same problem.
Matchsticks to Square, a nearly identical problem (partition into exactly 4 equal-length sides).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches share the same theoretical worst-case bound, but the descending-sort-plus-fail-fast-pruning version is dramatically faster in practice, which is what actually makes this problem tractable within the given constraints.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: backtracking with strong pruning, filling one equal-sum bucket at a time.
Core Idea: compute target = total/k, sort descending, fill buckets one at a time, prune overflowing additions and redundant empty-bucket first attempts.
Time: O(k^n) worst case in theory for both, but pruning makes the optimized version fast in practice.
Space: O(n) for the used array and recursion depth.
Most Important Observation: descending sort plus empty-bucket fail-fast pruning is what makes this backtracking problem practically tractable.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately hard backtracking problem prized for its pruning techniques.
One line memory trick: target = total/k; sort big to small; fill one bucket fully before starting the next.
